key_insight: From 2021 to 2026, medical-AI abstracts in top-tier journals became more critically evaluative, with Cautious Optimism still the dominant tone but a rising share of Alarm/Caution.
clinical_relevance: This suggests the medical literature is increasingly scrutinizing AI safety, error modes, and regulation, which may shape how clinicians interpret the trustworthiness and readiness of AI tools.
method: LLM-assisted content analysis of 97,492 Q1/Q2 medical journal records, retaining 16,759 discourse/evaluative abstracts.
Claude Sonnet 4.6 classified stance into Alarm, Caution, Neutral, Cautious Optimism, and Advocacy; annual trends used 16,747 records from 2021-2026.
Human validation showed good-to-strong agreement for stance and several annotation layers.
evidence_signal: Among 16,749 valid stance classifications, 30.8% were critical, with critical share rising from 25.4% to 32.6% and advocacy falling from 2.9% to 0.6%.
watch_item: Because the study relies on abstract-level, LLM-assisted coding and moderate agreement for some failure-mode labels, theme shifts—especially fabrication-related estimates—should be interpreted cautiously.
paper_title: Evaluative Stance Toward Artificial Intelligence in High-Quartile Medical Journals (2021-2026): Large-Scale LLM-Assisted Computational Content Analysis
